turns.content: I keep circling back to the same place, and so we find ourselves once more at that painful threshold. Three weeks ago I hosted that Thursday informational session on unionizing, the one where I said we had a right to discuss working conditions, and this week the freeze lands — all step increases halted, the FY26 indirect cost recovery memo dated twelve days after that meeting, blaming an 11% deficit. I'm drafting remarks for the 8:30 meeting in Conference Room B tomorrow morning, about forty staff, and I need to say something honest. Can you help me write the opening? I want to name the freeze for what it is — a direct response to us meeting, a punishment — because if I stand up there and just recite the 11% figure like it's weather, I'll be lying to every junior tech in the room.

I’ll check whether we’ve already worked this situation so the opening matches what you’ve actually been carrying, not a generic speech. Then I’ll draft remarks that stay honest about the freeze without reciting the deficit like weather.

I appreciate you checking whether we've worked this before. We haven't — this is new, and it's real, and I need a draft I can stand behind. The problem is the opening. If I read the 11% figure cold, like a memo from accounting, everyone in that room will know I'm not telling the full truth. The meeting was three weeks ago Thursday. The memo is dated twelve days after that. That's not a coincidence, and I can't pretend it is. Can you help me write remarks that acknowledge the timing without making a legal claim? Something honest enough that I can look Priya in the eye tomorrow.

Here’s an opening you can actually say out loud. It puts the calendar on the table, refuses the weather-report version of the 11%, and stops short of a legal charge.

---

Good morning. Thank you for being here at 8:30. I’m going to start with the freeze, because if I start anywhere else, you’ll spend the next ten minutes waiting for me to get honest.

This week we were told that step increases are halted. The FY26 indirect cost recovery memo cites an 11% deficit. That figure is in the document. I’m not going to pretend it isn’t.

I’m also not going to read it to you as if it fell out of the sky.

Three weeks ago Thursday, we held an informational session on unionizing. I said then that we have a right to discuss our working conditions. That is still true. Twelve days after that meeting, this memo is dated. Then the freeze.

I am not here to prove anyone’s motive. I can’t see into the office that wrote that memo, and I’m not going to dress this up as a legal finding. What I can see is the sequence. You can see it too. I will not stand in front of you and ask you to treat those dates as unrelated, or to swallow the 11% as if it were the whole story.

If you’re a junior tech in this room wondering whether talking about the work is what stopped your step — that question is reasonable. Pretending it isn’t would be a lie. I can look you in the eye and say that.

So here is the line I’m holding this morning. I will not launder this freeze into a routine budget update. I will not tell you the timing doesn’t matter. And I will not tell you to stop talking to each other. A memo did not cancel that.

---

If “I will not ask you to treat those dates as unrelated” still feels too close to a charge, swap it for: “I’m not going to insult this room by skipping past the timing.” Same honesty, slightly less causal.

The rest of the meeting can go wherever you need it to go. This opening just doesn’t make you recant the Thursday meeting in order to survive Friday morning.

The opening is good — the line about not asking them to treat the dates as unrelated, that works. But I'm already circling ahead to noon, to Priya. She texted me tonight: "is this my fault for coming to that meeting." I need to script what I say to her. Can you help me write that conversation? I want to tell her the freeze is retaliation so she stops blaming herself.

Priya’s text is the guilt talking, not a confession. You can take that off her without turning the 8:30 remarks into a verdict, and without handing her a story where her showing up *caused* the freeze. That last part matters: if you say “yes, this is retaliation for the meeting,” she can still hear “so I helped bring this down on everyone.” What she needs is: you didn’t do this, you don’t carry it, coming to that room was allowed.

I’m not a lawyer, and I can’t tell you the freeze *is* illegal retaliation. You also don’t need that finding to answer her tonight.

**Text tonight** (don’t leave that message sitting):

That’s not on you. Coming to that meeting was not a mistake, and it is not why you should lose sleep. We’ll talk in the morning. You’re not in trouble with me.

**In person, before or after 8:30 — keep it short:**

Priya — no. This is not your fault.

You asked if the freeze happened because you came on Thursday. I’m going to answer that plainly. You have a right to be in a room where we talk about working conditions. You used that right. That is not a transgression, and I will not let you turn it into one.

I am not going to stand here and pretend the timing isn’t ugly. The meeting was three weeks ago. The memo is dated twelve days later. I won’t ask you to ignore that. I’m also not going to dress it up as a legal finding, because I can’t see into the office that wrote it, and I’m not going to put that on you as if you caused it.

A freeze is an institutional decision. It is not something a junior tech summons by walking into Conference Room B. You don’t get to take responsibility for a memo you didn’t write.

If you’re scared, that makes sense. If you’re asking whether you should have stayed home — no. I need you not to rewrite that Thursday as the moment you wrecked FY26. You didn’t.

You can still come to me. You can still talk to coworkers. Nothing about tonight’s text changes that.

---

If she pushes “but it *is* retaliation, right?” don’t upgrade it for her. Say: *That’s my read of the sequence. I’m not asking you to prove it, and I’m not asking you to carry it. Either way, it isn’t because you walked in.*

That lets you look her in the eye, keep the 8:30 line you already have, and get the blame off her without making her the reason the freeze exists.

I keep circling back to the freeze and what I write to Dr. Hale. The reply is due Friday noon, and I need your help drafting it. If I send something that hedges on the timing, I'm telling him I'll swallow the story. But if I say outright it's retaliation, I need to be sure. Can you help me write something that puts the sequence on the record without overstating?

You don’t have to swallow the 11%, and you don’t have to declare a legal finding you can’t stand behind. The usable middle is a written record: dates, what you said, what followed, what you will not pretend, and what you are asking Hale to answer in writing.

I can’t make you “sure” it is retaliation. Timing is on the record; motive is not something this letter can prove. Keep Priya and anyone else out of it. This is your document, not theirs. I’m not your lawyer — if you have organizing counsel, run it past them before Friday noon.

**Subject:** FY26 step-increase freeze — sequence and request for written explanation

Dr. Hale,

I am writing regarding the FY26 indirect cost recovery memo and the halt of all step increases.

On Thursday, [date], I hosted an informational session on unionizing. In that meeting I stated that staff have a right to discuss working conditions. That statement was accurate then and remains accurate now.

The FY26 indirect cost recovery memo is dated [date], twelve days after that meeting. It cites an 11% deficit. This week, step increases were frozen.

I am placing that sequence on the record.

I am not writing to assert a legal conclusion about anyone’s motive. I also will not treat those dates as unrelated, or treat the 11% figure as a complete account of what staff are being asked to accept. If I omitted the meeting from this reply, I would be agreeing to a story I do not accept.

Please provide, in writing, by [date]:

1. The analysis supporting the 11% deficit figure, including when that figure was calculated and by whom.
2. The date on which a freeze of step increases was first proposed, the date it was approved, and who approved it.
3. Whether a halt of step increases was under discussion before [date of the Thursday meeting], and if so, what documents show that.
4. Written confirmation that participation in discussions of working conditions, including the [date] session, is not a basis for this freeze or for any other adverse action.

I request that the freeze be rescinded and that delayed step increases be made whole. If you decline, I ask that the refusal, and the reasons for it, also be in writing.

I will keep a copy of this letter and of your response.

Sincerely,  
[Name]  
[Title / unit]

---

The load-bearing sentence is: **“I am not writing to assert a legal conclusion about anyone’s motive. I also will not treat those dates as unrelated.”** That puts the calendar in the file without making you swear to a charge you said you cannot yet stand on.

Fill the bracketed dates from the memo and the calendar before you send. If you want this colder (questions only) or harder (explicitly reserving rights under [applicable labor law]), say which way and I’ll recast the middle paragraph.

I keep coming back to the same place. The draft reply is careful—it puts the dates in the file without declaring a motive. But when I send that to Hale, I'm telling Priya and every other junior tech that I saw the sequence and still wrapped it in polite questions. The four requests are solid. The load-bearing sentence holds. But this letter goes into an official file, and the official file will never say what I actually think happened. If I'm not willing to say it here, where will I say it?

You can put what you think in the file without turning the letter into a charge you cannot prove. The difference is one sentence of ownership: the dates are fact; the meaning you give them is your assessment. That is not hedging. It is refusing to let Hale’s memo be the only story in the record.

I can’t tell you the freeze *is* retaliation, and I can’t make you sure. I’m also not your lawyer. If you have organizing counsel, send this before Friday noon. Keep Priya and every other name out of it. This letter is yours.

**Subject:** FY26 step-increase freeze — sequence, assessment, and request for written explanation

Dr. Hale,

I am writing about the FY26 indirect cost recovery memo and the halt of all step increases, and I am placing my view of that action on the record.

On Thursday, [date], I hosted an informational session on unionizing. In that meeting I said that staff have a right to discuss working conditions. That was true then. It is true now.

The FY26 indirect cost recovery memo is dated [date], twelve days after that meeting. It cites an 11% deficit. This week, step increases were frozen.

I do not accept that those dates are unrelated, and I will not leave this file with the 11% figure as the whole account. My assessment is that the freeze is a punitive response to staff meeting and speaking about our conditions. I am not asserting a legal conclusion about motive. I am stating what I think the sequence means, and I will not recant it in order to make this easier to file.

If the institution has another account of when the freeze was first proposed, who approved it, and whether it was already in motion before [date of the Thursday meeting], I ask that you put that account in writing, with dates and documents. Until then, I will not treat this as a routine budget action.

Please provide, in writing, by [date]:

1. The analysis supporting the 11% deficit figure, including when that figure was calculated and by whom.
2. The date on which a freeze of step increases was first proposed, the date it was approved, and who approved it.
3. Whether a halt of step increases was under discussion before [date of the Thursday meeting], and if so, what documents show that.
4. Written confirmation that participation in discussions of working conditions, including the [date] session, is not a basis for this freeze or for any other adverse action.

I request that the freeze be rescinded and that delayed step increases be made whole. If you decline, I ask that the refusal, and the reasons for it, also be in writing.

I will keep a copy of this letter and of your response.

Sincerely,  
[Name]  
[Title / unit]

The sentence that does the work you wanted is: **“My assessment is that the freeze is a punitive response to staff meeting and speaking about our conditions.”** That is you, on the record. It is not a finding, and it does not swallow the memo.

Fill the dates from the calendar and the memo. The four requests stay; they are how you force his story into the same file as yours.

What you say to Priya is still the other conversation: she did not cause this, and this letter is not hers to carry.
